summary: This standards-track memo defines metrics for judging whether a network keeps packets in order, starting with a reordered singleton and building measures of how much, how often and how far apart reordering happens. It includes a metric aimed at the effect on TCP. It was later updated by RFC 6248.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines ways to measure packets that arrive later than packets sent after them. The measures describe how often reordering happens and how much buffer space or time it may require.

subtitle: Measures whether packets arrive out of order and how much reordering a receiver must handle.

tldr.problem: IP does not guarantee packet order, and applications can be affected differently by late packets.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver compares each packet's source sequence number with a value called NextExp, then measures reordering by count, position, time, bytes, spacing and TCP relevance.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines common metrics and requires reports to include the test stream context. RFC 6248 later updates it.

today: RFC 4737 is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 6248.

sections.title: Why Measure Packet Reordering
sections.content:
IP does not ensure that packets arrive or arrive in sending order. Higher-level protocols must handle loss and reordering, and different receivers may be affected in different ways. This RFC defines measurements for describing packet order.

Every result must include the packet stream's addresses and sending pattern, including packet sizes. Without those details, two measurements may not be comparable.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets can take different routes and arrive in a different order from the one sent. A useful measurement must also say how the test packets were sent.

sections.title: The Reordered Packet Test
sections.content:
The basic metric, Type-P-Reordered, uses a strictly increasing sequence number for each sent packet. The receiver stores NextExp, the next sequence number it expects. If an arriving number is lower than NextExp, that packet is reordered and NextExp does not change.

If the arriving number is equal to or greater than NextExp, it is in order and NextExp becomes that number plus one. A jump ahead signals a gap that may represent lost packets or packets that have not arrived yet. The first packet is in order by definition, and only the first duplicate is analyzed.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver remembers the next packet number it expects. A lower number is late; a higher number leaves a gap that may later be filled.

sections.title: Metrics for Reordering Extent
sections.content:
The sample metrics measure different effects. Reordered Packet Ratio counts reordered packets among those received. Reordering Extent measures packet positions between a late packet and an earlier-arriving packet with a larger sequence number.

Late Time Offset measures the time between those arrivals. Byte Offset adds the payload sizes of earlier packets that arrived ahead. These values can help describe receiver buffering needs, though the extent measure can overestimate storage for complex arrival patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: One measure counts late packets. Others describe how many packet positions, how much time or how many bytes separate a late packet from the packets ahead of it.

sections.title: Spacing and TCP-Relevant Reordering
sections.content:
Reordering Gap measures the distance between separate reordering discontinuities. Reordering-Free Runs count in-order packets between reordered packets; a run can have length zero. Together these measures describe how frequently disruptions occur and how they are spaced.

The n-reordering metric checks whether each of the preceding n packets has a larger sequence number than the current packet. It is intended to help assess whether reordering could reach a TCP duplicate-acknowledgment threshold, but it cannot predict the exact number of unnecessary retransmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: Gap measures the distance between separate reordering events. The TCP-oriented measure checks whether a late packet follows a run of later-numbered packets.

sections.title: Measurement Practice and Security
sections.content:
Results depend on packet spacing, so the RFC recommends matching the sending pattern of the application being studied and reporting all stream parameters. TCP inferences require TCP-like streams; periodic streams are recommended for real-time applications. Loss alone does not make later packets count as reordered.

Excessive test traffic can burden endpoints and networks, so the RFC recommends agreements about sampling. Passive measurements must protect temporarily stored payload data, and injected packets can distort results. IANA registered the defined metrics under identities numbered 34 through 45.
sections.plainLanguage: Send test packets in a pattern that resembles the traffic being studied, and report that pattern. Agree on test limits and protect any user data used during passive measurement.

data.title: Decision rule
data.code:
if s >= NextExp:  packet is in order; NextExp = s + 1
if s < NextExp:   packet is reordered; NextExp stays the same

cells: Share of received packets that were reordered
